propositions.text: Backup generator G2 at the Harrow Basin pumping station shut down at 02:14 on the night of the storm.

The shutdown was caused by a low coolant level trip.
The shutdown was caused by a clogged fuel filter starving the engine.
Three of the five drainage pumps lost power when the generator stopped.
Four of the five drainage pumps lost power when the generator stopped.
The generator's coolant temperature gauge read 108 degrees Celsius just before shutdown.
The outage lasted 11 minutes before power was restored.
Power was restored by switching the station to the secondary grid feed.
The main grid supply had failed at 20:30 the previous evening, which is why the generator was running.
Rainfall at the time of the shutdown measured 18 millimeters per hour.
Water in the collection basin rose by 22 centimeters during the outage.
The basin level did not reach the 3.5 meter overflow alarm threshold.
An audible alarm sounded in the control room for the duration of the outage.
The generator's fuel tank held about 60 percent of its capacity at the time of the shutdown.
The generator had last received a full service 14 months earlier.
Only one operator was on duty in the control room at the time.
The generator was restarted manually at 03:02 and ran without further faults until dawn.
The generator's housing was found warm to the touch but showed no sign of fire or smoke.
A full inspection of the generator was scheduled for the following Tuesday.
Generator G1 at the Calder Reach grain terminal shut down at 15:42 during the loading of the freighter Marisol.

The shutdown was triggered by a high coolant temperature alarm.
The shutdown was triggered by a low oil pressure trip.
The outdoor air temperature at the time was 37 degrees Celsius.

Four conveyor lines lost power when the generator stopped.
Three conveyor lines lost power when the generator stopped.

The automatic transfer switch did not connect the grid supply because the grid feed had been disconnected for cable work that day.
Emergency lighting in the control room came on within two seconds.
Maintenance staff opened the radiator access panels at 15:50.
A layer of grain dust was found covering the radiator fins.
The generator was restarted at 16:31.
Conveyor loading resumed at 16:40.
The total outage of loading lasted 58 minutes.
The radiator had last been cleaned 19 days earlier.
The coolant level in the expansion tank was found at normal level after the stop.
The freighter Marisol was scheduled to leave the berth at 20:00.

The standby generator at the Vellmoor Ridge observatory shut down at 21:37 on the evening of the winter power cut.

The generator had started automatically eleven seconds after the mains failure.
The generator ran for 32 minutes before it shut down.
The generator shut down because its fuel filter was blocked by ice-clogged diesel.
The generator shut down because its coolant level sensor triggered a low-coolant trip.
The outside air temperature at the time of shutdown was minus 19 degrees Celsius.
The generator's fuel tank gauge read 40 percent full at the last check before the shutdown.
Battery backup took over the dome controls with no gap in supply.

Seven staff members were on site when the generator stopped.
Four staff members were on site when the generator stopped.
The night operator closed the dome shutter by hand-triggered command at 21:44.
The telescope's cooling system for its camera was switched off at 21:50 to save battery power.
The Engine Control Panel recorded an oil pressure reading of 3.8 bar just before the stop.
The maintenance technician arrived at the generator shed at 22:10.
The generator was restarted manually at 22:52 after the fuel filter was replaced.
Mains power returned to the observatory at 23:30.
The generator had last been serviced 14 months before the event.
Battery voltage had dropped to 78 percent of full charge by the time mains power returned.
Generator M1 at the Tessaly Fen water-treatment annex shut down at 04:51 on the foggy morning of the aeration cycle.

The shutdown was caused by a clogged fuel filter that starved the engine.
The shutdown was caused by a failed coolant pump that triggered the overheat trip.
Four aeration basins lost power when M1 stopped.
Six aeration basins lost power when M1 stopped.
The engine temperature gauge read 118 degrees Celsius just before the trip.
M1 had accumulated 1,846 running hours since its last service.
The fuel tank was recorded at 62 percent full at 04:00.
Visibility at the annex gate was about 40 meters because of the fog.
The low-voltage alarm sounded at 04:52, one minute after the shutdown.
The shift engineer was in the switch room when the engine stopped.
A fuel-filter replacement was listed as due but not yet done.
The smaller backup unit M2 was started by hand at 05:09.

Aeration was off for 47 minutes in total.
Dissolved oxygen in the main basin fell from 3.4 to 1.1 milligrams per liter during the outage.
Grid power returned to the annex at 05:38.
The blowers were restarted one at a time after grid power returned.
The effluent turbidity reading stayed within permitted limits through the morning.
Generator K3 at the Ostrel Quay cold-storage warehouse shut down at 11:26 during the afternoon grid outage.

The outdoor temperature at the loading dock read 34 degrees Celsius at the time of the shutdown.

A technician restarted K3 manually at 12:31.

The generator's oil pressure alarm did not sound before the stop.
Chamber A, which holds crab, stayed below minus 20 degrees Celsius throughout.
The warehouse manager ordered the dock doors kept shut for the whole outage.

The fan belt on K3 was replaced the following morning.
No fish were discarded as a result of the outage.

A repair crew of five arrived at the site at 4:58 a.m.

The utility's engineering report said the failure was caused by a corroded joint collar that gave way at the bell end.
The pipe was installed in 1931 according to the asset register.
The asset register lists the failed section as 214 feet long.
Crews closed two isolation valves, the second at 5:41 a.m., which stopped the flow.
The foreman counted 11 rowhouses with water in their basements.

Water reached a depth of about 14 inches at the lowest point of the intersection.
The flooding forced the closure of Teller Lane between Brandt Street and the bridge.

The customer call center counted 265 households on Kiln Hill without service.
A boil-water advisory was issued for the affected neighborhood at 6:30 p.m.
The pipe section was installed in 1987.
The failed section was a 9-foot length of pipe that crews replaced with a new spool piece.
The basement of a corner bakery took on about two inches of water.
A flow meter on the main showed no reading after 2:47 p.m. until the valves were reopened.
Service was restored to the first homes at 11:15 p.m.
The road surface above the break sank about eight inches before crews cut it open.
The last valve was reopened and the advisory lifted two days later at 9:00 a.m. on Monday.

The pressure sensor at Valve Station 9 recorded a drop from 68 psi to 21 psi within four minutes.

The crew arrived at the loading yard at 10:20 p.m.
The break was caused by a corroded weld seam that had been patched during an earlier repair.
The break was caused by a forklift striking an exposed fitting on the pipe's upper surface.
Water covered the loading yard to an average depth of about 8 inches.
Water flowed onto the adjoining rail spur and covered the tracks for roughly 150 feet.
Crews closed the two isolation valves bracketing the break by 11:05 p.m.
Flow from the break stopped after the valves closed at 11:05 p.m.
Eleven pallets of frozen goods stored on the ground-level dock were soaked.
Twenty-six pallets of frozen goods stored on the ground-level dock were soaked.
About 34 homes on Pellam Street lost water service during the repair.
The utility estimated that 310,000 gallons escaped before the valves were closed.
Rail traffic on the spur was halted until the next morning.
The rail dispatcher held one freight car of packaging materials at the spur entrance.
The damaged section of pipe, about 12 feet long, was cut out and replaced.
Water service to Pellam Street was restored at 4:30 a.m. on Friday.
The adjuster inspected the loading yard at noon on Friday and found a pooled residue of silt along the dock wall.
At 11:20 a.m. on a Monday in April, a 30-inch prestressed concrete cylinder water main burst beneath the Corvane Rail Underpass.
The pressure sensor at the Sable Hill pumping station dropped from 68 psi to 41 psi within four minutes of the burst.
The first emergency call about water coming up through the pavement was logged at 11:24 a.m.
The dispatcher logged nine calls about the flooding in the first twenty minutes.
The burst was caused by corroded steel wire wrapping around the pipe core that had failed.
The burst was caused by ground settling after nearby track-bed excavation work undermined the pipe's support.
About 140 households lost water service as a result of the shutdown.
About 230 households lost water service as a result of the shutdown.

A delivery van stalled in the floodwater and its driver walked out unharmed.
The rail authority halted commuter trains through the underpass at 11:42 a.m.
Trains resumed at reduced speed at 6:10 p.m. the same day.
Crews closed the two isolation valves on Pell Street at 12:05 p.m.
The flow meter downstream of the break showed flow falling to zero at 12:07 p.m.

The pipe was installed in 1964.

Water was heard roaring under the road several minutes before the pavement lifted.
The utility set up two tanker trucks of drinking water at the Pell Street lot by 2:00 p.m.
Repairs were completed and service restored at 4:30 a.m. the following Wednesday.

Fourteen workers were on the night shift when the alarm sounded.

The first fire engine arrived at the gate at 02:26.
Firefighters called for two additional engines at 02:40.

A thermal camera on the east wall recorded a peak temperature of 640 degrees Celsius at 02:50.

The first fire engine arrived at the depot at 19:53.
Firefighters brought the fire under control at 21:10.

The temperature sensor in Aisle 14 recorded a peak of 412 degrees Celsius at 20:05.

Aisle 14 had been restocked with new solvent drums that afternoon.

At 04:37 on June 17, a fire started in the battery charging bay of the Fenwick Quay Parcel Warehouse.
The smoke detector in the charging bay triggered the first alarm at 04:37.

About 1,800 bales of cardboard were destroyed.

The temperature sensor near the hall ceiling recorded 212 degrees Celsius at 13:31.
Two workers were treated at the scene for smoke inhalation.
